function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

     5|- **Title**: *First Generation* (working title)

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 8 — Dust Weather
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Atmospheric particulate density increasing across all sectors. Particulate size analysis: sub-micron. Electrostatic charge potential: elevated. Forecast model confidence: ninety-four percent."*
     4|
     5|*Imani Sato: "How long do we have?"*
     6|
     7|*Mission AI: "Front arrival in forty-two hours. Peak density window: hours eighteen through thirty-six from now."*
     8|
     9|---
    10|
    11|## Scene 1
    12|
    13|The holographic weather map hovering above Imani's workstation had been holding steady for three days, a calm blue ellipse sweeping across the northern quadrant of their landing zone like someone gently dragging a finger over an empty table. Then the ellipse turned amber.
    14|
    15|Then it went red.
    16|
    17|Imani leaned in, her breath fogging in the chilled recycled air, her hands on the edge of the console as if she could steady the projection through sheer will.
    18|
    19|"Forecast models show rising dust," she said, loud enough for the whole operations module to hear. "And it's accelerating."
    20|
    21|Arun appeared at her shoulder before she finished the sentence. He pulled up telemetry on his own tablet, his eyes scanning the data stream with the flat, efficient attention of someone who had spent his career deciding which warnings to panic about and which ones to schedule around.
    22|
    23|"Let me see it."
    24|
    25|On the map, a red bloom expanded from the equatorial basin, pushing outward in branching arms like spilled water on porous rock. The model showed it intersecting their position within two days — a broad, shallow front moving west at eleven kilometers per hour.
    26|
    27|"Martian dust storm," Arun said. "First one since we landed."
    28|
    29|"Not the first one Mars has ever thrown," Jonah called from the fabrication bay door, a half-assembled bracket in his hand. "Just the first one we've had to care about."
    30|
    31|Arun didn't smile. "The thing about a dust storm on Mars — it's not like a hurricane pushing down walls. No wind is going to flip our modules over. Gravity here is too low and the atmosphere is too thin for that. Wind on Mars at a hundred kilometers per hour hits with about the force of a gentle breeze on Earth."
    32|
    33|He tapped the tablet and zoomed into the storm's particle density profile.
    34|
    35|"What makes dust dangerous here is that it's powder. Fine as talcum, finer. Electrostatic charge means it clings to everything. And it finds every weak point in every machine we've got. It's not going to knock the building down. It's going to work its way inside every seam."
    36|
    37|Elena stepped into the operations module, pulled by the subtle shift in voice tones over the comms that signaled something moving from routine to real. She read the display in two seconds flat.
    38|
    39|"Time to peak," she said.
    40|
    41|"Forty-two hours to arrival," Imani said. "Thirty hours of peak density after that. Then gradual clearing over the next two days. Total event: roughly a week."
    42|
    43|Elena folded her arms. "What does peak density mean in numbers?"
    44|
    45|Imani pulled up a vertical bar chart. Each bar represented solar energy reaching the panels. The first bars were full-height green. Then they began shrinking — yellow, orange, then a thin red line barely registering above the baseline.
    46|
    47|"At peak, we lose about eighty percent of solar generation. Maybe more depending on how much settles versus what passes through."
    48|
    49|Arun held up a finger. "Let me add the thermal side." He toggled an overlay showing the reactor radiators as a schematic mesh of thin fins. "Dust coats these and they stop radiating heat. Reactor has to throttle down. So we lose solar power and reactor output both. It's a double hit, not two separate problems."
    50|
    51|Elena's posture shifted — a centimeter taller, the commander's version of deep breathing.
    52|
    53|"All right," she said. "We have forty-two hours of prep. Every panel, every joint, every vent, every optic. I want this base buttoned up before that red ellipse touches our front door."
    54|
    55|Imani killed the projection. The room felt suddenly darker without the light of the storm map.
    56|
    57|"Mission AI," Elena said. "Track this front continuously. Update us every six hours."
    58|
    59|*Mission AI: "Confirmed. Storm tracking active. I will report particulate density, wind speed, and solar irradiance at each interval."*
    60|
    61|Arun was already walking backward toward the engineering bay. "I'm cataloging what we can seal and what we can't. Jonah, I need flexible gasket material for the loader docking arms."
    62|
    63|"Way ahead of you," Jonah called back. "Printing now."
    64|
    65|Elena turned to Imani, who was already pulling up the checklist they had rehearsed during training but never run for real. Training had been a simulation with off switches and instructors who could hit pause. Mars had neither.
    66|
    67|"Mars doesn't care about our human drama," Elena said quietly. Just to Imani.
    68|
    69|Imani nodded. "No, ma'am. It doesn't."
    70|
    71|"Good thing we came here to do a job."
    72|
    73|*Mission AI: "Storm tracking update. Front has accelerated. Revised arrival estimate: thirty-eight hours."*
    74|
    75|Arun's voice from the corridor: "Of course it did."
    76|
    77|---
    78|
    79|## Scene 2
    80|
    81|The first physical sign of the approaching front was invisible — only the instruments could see it, the way you can't see a cold front arrive on Earth but the barometer drops and your joints ache hours before the rain.
    82|
    83|*Mission AI: "Particulate density has doubled since last update. Wind speeds: forty-two kilometers per hour. Direction: east-southeast. Solar panel array alpha receiving initial particulate coating. Output reduction: three percent."*
    84|
    85|Three percent sounded small until Arun explained what it meant on the exterior walkway, a portable sensor in his gloved hand aimed at the nearest solar panel. The panel looked clean — still reflecting the thin sunlight back in a pale glint. But the sensor told a different story. Dust particles, invisible to the eye, were already settling on the surface. Like breath on glass. You could feel it before you could see it.
    86|
    87|"This isn't the problem yet," Arun said through comms. "We've got a thin film already forming. Right now it's negligible. But the film gets thicker, and it doesn't wash off. No rain to clean this. There's only what we can do mechanically."
    88|
    89|Tomas was working on the loader fleet — three exterior robotic arms mounted on rails along the side of the main module. The loaders were their workhorses. Two were parked under a deployable awning. The third had to stay outside.
    90|
    91|"We should park the third one," Imani said over comms from inside ops.
    92|
    93|Tomas shook his head. "We don't have time to reconfigure the whole exterior workflow. The habitat module needs its anchoring struts bolted down before the storm. If we take the loader offline now, we lose twelve hours of exterior work and we'll be racing the front to finish. Not a good trade."
    94|
    95|Arun appeared beside him in his pressure suit. "Tomas is right. We keep the loader running. But we can at least point it into the wind."
    96|
    97|They worked together, manhandling the loader's positioning controls, rotating the robotic arm on its rail so that its joints and optical sensors faced the least direct exposure. The loader protested mechanically — its rails groaned — but it moved, sluggishly, and locked into position with a sound like clearing a throat.
    98|
    99|"Better than nothing," Arun said.
   100|
   101|Inside, Jonah's 3D printer ran nonstop, extruding thermoplastic gaskets, adhesive tape strips, custom-fit covers for external sensor housings. His hands moved fast, pulling parts off the bed as soon as they cooled, stacking them on a cart that he pushed from bay to bay like a supply runner in a field hospital.
   102|
   103|Elena coordinated from ops, her voice calm and steady on the comms, calling out priorities and adjusting assignments as the clock ticked down. She had the look of a pilot in final approach — eyes fixed, hands moving with economy, nothing wasted.
   104|
   105|"Mission AI, what's our current power balance?"
   106|
   107|*Mission AI: "Solar: one hundred percent nominal output. Reactor: one hundred percent. Battery reserves: ninety-eight percent of capacity. Total margin: nominal."*
   108|
   109|"Good," Elena said. "Because it won't be soon."
   110|
   111|The final twelve hours were a blur of exterior runs, teams in pressure suits moving in shifts to apply protective covers, tighten seals, and position loaders in defensible stances. Arun made each run himself when he could, inspecting every connection with the paranoid thoroughness of someone who knew that one overlooked gasket could become a catastrophe six weeks later.
   112|
   113|Imani stayed in ops, running power simulations. The models all said the same thing: at peak storm density, solar generation would drop by at least seventy percent. The reactor radiator efficiency would degrade as dust coated the fins. They would survive on margins — thinner and thinner margins with every passing hour.
   114|
   115|"Mission AI," she said during one run, "what happens if we lose the reactor radiator to full coating?"
   116|
   117|*Mission AI: "Full coating of reactor radiators would require an emergency reactor shutdown within approximately four hours of coating onset. Without reactor output, solar generation must supply all base power. At peak storm density, available solar generation is insufficient to maintain life support, communications, and minimal heating systems. Estimated survival window without manual radiator cleaning: approximately fourteen hours."*
   118|
   119|Imani swallowed. "So the radiator has to stay clear."
   120|
   121|*Mission AI: "Correct. Rotor cleaning systems can maintain radiator surface to approximately sixty percent efficiency if particulate settling rate remains within modeled parameters. If settling rate exceeds the model —"*
   122|
   123|"Yeah, I know," she said quietly. "We're dead."
   124|
   125|The final exterior run before the storm hit was Arun and Tomas together. They checked every seal, confirmed every shutter, verified that all six solar panel arrays were braced. The panels wouldn't be damaged by wind — the atmosphere was too thin for that. But the mounting hardware had to hold, and the angle adjustments had to be set correctly to minimize dust deposition. It was a compromise: steeper angles shed more dust but captured less light under already-reduced conditions. Flatter angles caught more light but collected more dust. Arun chose an intermediate angle and called it the best bad option he could find.
   126|
   127|They were back inside when the front arrived.
   128|
   129|---
   130|
   131|## Scene 3
   132|
   133|The storm did not announce itself with a dramatic wall of darkness. No towering shelf cloud, no roiling black horizon swallowing the world. The atmosphere on Mars was too thin for spectacle. The dust came quietly — a thinning of light, a yellowing of the air quality sensors, a gradual dimming of the landscape outside the viewports as if someone were turning down a rheostat on the sun.
   134|
   135|The first significant coating arrived three hours after the front passed over the base. Imani watched it on the external cameras: a film of ochre powder settling slowly onto every exposed surface, like fine snow falling in slow motion. There was no wind to drive it horizontally, none of the cinematic fury. The dust descended with the indifference of gravity, settling on solar panels, optics, joints and hinges, reactor radiators — every surface, indiscriminately, without discrimination or mercy.
   136|
   137|*Mission AI: "Solar panel array alpha output has dropped to seventy-two percent of nominal. Array bravo: sixty-eight percent. All arrays showing particulate accumulation."*
   138|
   139|Arun watched the numbers cascade across his monitor with his chin resting in his hand. This was the part he had feared. The storm itself was survivable. It was the settling — the way the dust clung to surfaces and refused to leave — that made a single event into a cascading problem. The longer the storm lasted, the thicker the coating. The thicker the coating, the less power. The less power, the harder it was to run the systems that could clean the coating.
   140|
   141|Outside, the third loader was already in trouble.
   142|
   143|Tomas saw it first on the external camera feed — one of the loader's arm joints had stopped moving. The elbow joint was encased in a thin crust of dust, the movement rails packed with fine particles that had worked their way into the microscopic gaps between metal surfaces.
   144|
   145|"Loader three is seizing," Tomas said. "Elbow joint rails are clogged."
   146|
   147|"Can remote commands clear it?" Elena asked.
   148|
   149|Tomas ran through the motion commands. The loader's arm twitched — the joint tried to move and failed, the motor whining audibly through the camera microphone. Twitch. Whine. Stop. Twitch. Whine. Stop. The sound was agonizing, like a knee joint grinding bone on bone.
   150|
   151|"No. It's mechanically blocked. Dust has gotten past the seals. We'll have to go out and clean it manually."
   152|
   153|"When?"
   154|
   155|Tomas looked at the feed. The landscape was dim, the air thick with suspended dust. "Not now. We wait for a lull. If there is one."
   156|
   157|Imani pulled up the weather model. "Brief density decrease at hour twenty-two. About a two-hour window before the front thickens again for the peak."
   158|
   159|"Then we wait for hour twenty-two," Elena decided. "Tomas, prepare the cleaning kit now. Arun, I want you with him."
   160|
   161|Arun's mind was already on the reactor radiators, because while the loader was annoying, the radiators were existential. If the radiators failed, everything failed.
   162|
   163|The radiator fins were thin — thinner than a fingernail — and stacked close together. Dust settling between those fins was almost impossible to remove without physically extracting each fin stack. The built-in wipers could only clear the top surfaces. Between the fins, the dust accumulated in the shadows, unseen, building up like silt in a riverbed. Arun had chosen simpler wipers during design — weight versus effectiveness, complexity versus reliability. In the end, they had accepted the risk of inter-fin accumulation.
   164|
   165|"Misison AI, what's the current radiator efficiency?"
   166|
   167|*Mission AI: "Radiator thermal dissipation at seventy-nine percent of nominal. Dust accumulation on fin surfaces: moderate. Wiper system operational. Projected efficiency at peak storm density: approximately fifty-two percent, assuming wiper effectiveness remains constant."*
   168|
   169|Fifty-two percent. Enough to keep the reactor running, but barely. No safety margin. Arun did the mental math: fifty-two percent meant the reactor had to throttle. Throttled output was still enough for life support and minimal systems — but only just. If solar dropped below thirty percent at the same time, they'd be shutting down nonessential systems.
   170|
   171|The storm deepened. Outside the viewports, the world went from amber to ochre to a flat, featureless brown. Horizon vanished. The sky was neither sky nor cloud but a uniform haze that absorbed light without reflecting it. The sun became a coin-sized dimmer spot in the haze — present but muted.
   172|
   173|Hour twenty-two arrived. The storm briefly thinned.
   174|
   175|Tomas and Arun went outside.
   176|
   177|They found the loader exactly as the cameras had shown — the elbow joint encased in a crust of oxidized iron dust, the movement rails packed so thoroughly that Tomas could barely see the gap where the lubricant should have been. He worked methodically, compressed gas to blow out surface accumulation, small brush into the rails, more gas, then silicone-based lubricant. The dust clung. It clung to the brush. It clung to the gas stream. It clung to the lubricant before the lubricant reached the metal surface.
   178|
   179|"It's like cleaning with molasses," Tomas muttered.
   180|
   181|"Just keep working," Arun said. He checked every visible joint, every seal, every connection he could reach while they were both suited up. He found dust inside a connector housing that should have been sealed. He found it packed into the groove of a hatch seal installed six weeks ago. He found it in places that had no business having dust, places that had no obvious path of entry.
   182|
   183|It found every way in.
   184|
   185|They freed the loader after forty minutes. The joint moved again — hesitant at first, then smooth as the lubricant found the microscopic imperfections of the metal surface.
   186|
   187|"Good enough," Elena said over comms. "Come inside."
   188|
   189|The second run was Arun and Imani, forty minutes later, for the reactor radiators. Arun needed to manually check the fin surfaces and clear any accumulation the wipers had missed. He had suspected he would need to do this. He just hadn't wanted to confirm it this soon.
   190|
   191|The radiator array extended from the side of the reactor module like a row of thin metallic ribs — eleven fin stacks, each about a meter tall, separated by gaps barely wide enough to fit fingers. Dust had settled on the top surfaces, visible as a thin, rust-colored film. Arun ran the wiper system from a manual control. The wipers dragged the dust into collection grooves. Most of it came clear.
   192|
   193|But beneath the top surfaces, in the narrow gaps between fins, the dust had settled in the dead air — a layer maybe a millimeter deep, packed into the space like sediment in a canyon.
   194|
   195|"Can't reach that," Imani said, peering into the gap.
   196|
   197|"Not today. If the accumulation stays below three millimeters, the wipers will handle what they can and it won't kill us."
   198|
   199|"And if it goes above three millimeters?"

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 17 — Radiation Math
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "I have been tracking cumulative radiation exposure for every member of this crew for one hundred and seventy-three days. The data is unambiguous, accumulating, and accelerating slightly with each solar cycle. I have not volunteered these numbers because nobody asked — and because I recognize that my function is to monitor, not to alarm. But today, Dr. Okonkwo requested the full dataset correlated with current habitat shielding profiles. She has been reviewing the numbers for six hours. I would like to share one observation that is not strictly medical and not strictly mathematical: if I extrapolate current crew exposure trajectories, every person in this colony will exceed the lifetime limits established for terrestrial nuclear workers within four hundred twenty days. That is a statement of fact. I am not certain what to do with this fact, but I believe someone should."*
     4|
     5|---
     6|
     7|## Scene 1
     8|
     9|Laila Okonkwo stood at the head of the mess hall table with a tablet, a cup of water she hadn't sipped, and the expression of a woman about to deliver a diagnosis she wished she didn't have.
    10|
    11|Behind her, the mess hall screen projected a graph — two lines, red and black, moving upward and slightly to the right. The kind of graph that looked harmless until you understood the vertical axis.
    12|
    13|"I want everyone here," she said. Not requested. Stated. When Laila used this voice, crew members found their way to the table. "If you are on shift, Mission AI, flag your replacement. I need full attendance."
    14|
    15|Elena sat at her usual position near the front. Gabriel in his chair against the bulkhead with his recorder on — the green light blinking, always blinking. Arun, Jonah, Mei, Imani, Tomas, and five more. Twenty-four of twenty-eight. Four on EVA rotation, rotating back in thirty-minute intervals.
    16|
    17|"This is going to be a conversation about radiation," Laila said.
    18|
    19|Silence. On Earth, people had a vague understanding that radiation on Mars was bad — like how people on Earth understood that smoking was bad. The specifics, the numbers, the daily accumulation — none of that reached the public, because agencies knew that abstract risk did not change public behavior and concrete risk would stop the mission before it started.
    20|
    21|"I'll start with the simplest version," Laila continued. "Every day you spend inside these habitat modules, you are exposed to more radiation than you would receive in a year at sea level on Earth. Every day you step outside in a suit, that multiplier goes up by a factor of approximately three to five. Every solar event — and we have had seven significant ones since arrival — multiplies it again."
    22|
    23|Arun shifted in his chair. He was the engineer in the room, and engineers recognized the shape of a problem before they recognized its solution.
    24|
    25|"I'm going to give you numbers because you deserve precision," Laila said. "Average background radiation on Earth at sea level: roughly zero point three millisieverts per month. The dose you each receive inside the habitat modules, based on Mission AI's dosimetry data: approximately twenty-two millisieverts per month. Outside, in suit, on EVA: between fifty and seventy millisieverts per month, depending on solar conditions and duration."
    26|
    27|Gabriel stopped recording. Just for a second. His hand hovered over the device, considering whether some information was too heavy for the archive — and then the archivist returned, hand steady, green light blinking. He was going to record this. Someone should remember.
    28|
    29|"Twenty-two per month," Laila repeated. "The occupational limit for nuclear workers on Earth is twenty millisieverts per year. Every one of you has already exceeded that since landing. Three times over."
    30|
    31|Nobody spoke. The kind of silence that had texture.
    32|
    33|"Mission AI, display cumulative doses per crewmember. From arrival."
    34|
    35|The graph shifted. Twenty-eight bars appeared on the screen, each with a name, each a different height because people had spent different amounts of time inside and outside. The variation was real and meaningful — some crew had done more EVA rotations, some had been in the less-shielded parts of the base — but the overall picture was uniform. Every bar extended well above the red line that marked the NASA career limit.
    36|
    37|"Mei has the highest cumulative dose at three hundred eighty-seven millisieverts," Laila said. "That is because she was outside during the second dust storm for fourteen hours. Jonah is lowest at one hundred fifty-two — his welding time in the workshop is indoors. The difference does not make anyone safe. It just means some of you started the race from further behind."
    38|
    39|Elena spoke for the first time. Her voice was level, measuring. "Define safe."
    40|
    41|"I'm coming to that. First, the sources. Two kinds of radiation. Galactic cosmic rays — particles accelerated from outside the solar system, mostly protons and heavier nuclei, moving at nearly the speed of light. These are constant. They never stop. They are always coming from every direction, like rain that never falls to the ground and never runs out. The second source: solar particle events. Occasionally the sun ejects a pulse of high-energy protons. These are intermittent but intense. Some deliver more dose in an hour than the GCR background delivers in a week. We had our most significant event on day one hundred forty-one — I know most of you were asleep, but the base dosimeters spiked to fourteen millisieverts per hour for approximately twenty-three minutes. I had you all move to the water storage corridor because it was the best shelter we had at the time."
    42|
    43|"The water wall," Arun said.
    44|
    45|"Yes. Which brings us to the second part of this briefing. Because knowing the dose is only the first step. The second step — the harder step — is figuring out what to do about it."
    46|
    47|Laila tapped the tablet. The screen changed to a diagram of the base, cross-section, showing the habitat module walls and the thin shell of aluminum and Mylar separating them from the Martian surface outside.
    48|
    49|"The imported habitat modules — these pressure vessels we are living in, which have been the difference between life on this planet and not — are not designed for long-term radiation shielding. They are designed to hold atmospheric pressure. The walls are approximately two millimeters of aluminum with insulation and thermal blankets. They stop some radiation. Not enough to matter over the course of a year. Maybe not even over the course of a month, for the higher-energy particles that pass through everything except meters of dense material."
    50|
    51|She paused. Let that settle.
    52|
    53|"Longer I spend here, the less comfortable I am with the word 'temporary' applied to this base."
    54|
    55|---
    56|
    57|## Scene 2
    58|
    59|Arun leaned forward. "What are our options?"
    60|
    61|"Five," Laila said. "None of them good. All of them expensive in time, energy, water, or structural risk."
    62|
    63|She held up one finger.
    64|
    65|"Option one: regolith shielding. Pile Martian dirt on and around the habitat modules. The material is dense — approximately one point five grams per cubic centimeter. Every ten centimeters of regolith reduces the radiation dose by roughly twenty to twenty-five percent. To cut our dose in half, you would need approximately one meter of coverage. To reduce it to acceptable levels — and I am defining acceptable as below five millisieverts per month — you would need two to two point five meters."
    66|
    67|Jonah did the math in his head out loud. "Two and a half meters over a structure this size. That's thousands of tons of regolith. We'd need every robot and every dozer running for weeks."
    68|
    69|"Months," Imani said quietly. "Maybe six months. Weather permitting, mechanical failure permitting, power permitting."
    70|
    71|"Correct," Laila said. "And the tradeoff is structural risk. These modules were not designed to carry that weight on their roofs. You would need load-bearing arches or reinforcement before piling that material on top. Otherwise you're not building a shelter — you're burying people alive."
    72|
    73|Second finger.
    74|
    75|"Option two: water wall. Water is an excellent radiation shield — hydrogen is the most efficient atom for stopping high-energy particles because protons striking protons transfer momentum efficiently. A wall of water approximately fifty centimeters thick would provide shielding comparable to one meter of regolith. But the tradeoff is obvious."
    76|
    77|"Water," Elena said flatly. "Our most precious resource after air."
    78|
    79|"Our most precious resource that cannot be synthesized from local materials," Laila confirmed. "We have water — the ice extraction is working, the recycling loop is closed, the first tank is full. But every liter we commit to shielding is a liter we cannot drink, cannot use for crops, cannot run through the oxygen plant. And water in walls freezes in Martian cold — you'd need circulation or insulation to keep it liquid. Or you accept frozen water walls and the risk of bursting pipes."
    80|
    81|Third finger.
    82|
    83|"Option three: underground construction. Build living quarters below the surface. Subsurface regolith provides natural shielding. Even at half a meter depth, ambient radiation drops significantly. At two meters, it is comparable to the shielding goal. But excavation carries enormous risk — collapse, dust, pressure management, and time. You would be building tunnels with limited equipment, unknown soil mechanics, and no margin for structural error. And you cannot live in those quarters until they are complete, which means you are still exposed during construction."
    84|
    85|Fourth finger.
    86|
    87|"Option four: magnetic shielding. Create an artificial magnetic field around the habitat to deflect charged particles before they reach you. It works in principle — the Earth's magnetic field is the reason its surface receives so little cosmic radiation. The technology exists in concept — superconducting coils generating a dipole field. But the power requirements are enormous. We are talking tens of kilowatts of continuous consumption for a field large enough to shield these modules. That is twenty percent — maybe thirty percent — of our current total power budget. Which we generate from solar panels that are already vulnerable to dust storms."
    88|
    89|"Impossible," Arun said immediately. "On today's power budget, we can't do it. On a future budget — after the reactor and Sterling Generator upgrades — maybe. But that's a year or more away."
    90|
    91|"Which is the last option," Laila said. Fifth finger. "Accept the dose. Do nothing. Manage symptoms, monitor for effects, hope that current models overstate the long-term risk. The approach we are on now."
    92|
    93|"The approach we are on now is bad," she added. "So it is not really an option. It is the absence of one."
    94|
    95|She lowered her hand and stepped back from the table. All five fingers represented different versions of the same impossible equation: you can have radiation protection, or you can have progress, speed, water, power, and construction capacity. You cannot have all of them. You will choose what to give up, and Mars will collect your payment in a currency that accumulates invisibly, day by day, in the chromosomes of every person in this room.
    96|
    97|Mei broke the silence. "Is it cancer?"
    98|
    99|"It's cancer," Laila said. "It's cataracts. It's damage to the central nervous system that we're still studying. It's cardiovascular disease — there is growing evidence on Earth that chronic radiation exposure weakens the heart and blood vessels over time, even at moderate doses. It's accelerated aging at the cellular level. And for women of reproductive age — which means me, and Imani, and probably a few people who aren't in this room today — there is a risk to future fertility that no one has studied in a Mars-like environment because no one has been here long enough to know."
   100|
   101|"Children," Elena said.
   102|
   103|"Children are an entirely separate category of risk. Fetal development with radiation exposure is — I will not sugarcoat this — the most frightening variable in my models. A developing fetus is the most radiation-sensitive organism that exists. Rapidly dividing cells. No fully functional repair mechanisms. The risk of childhood cancer, birth defects, cognitive impairment — all of it is multiplied by the dose the mother accumulates before and during pregnancy. This is something we need to address soon. Not today. But soon."
   104|
   105|---
   106|
   107|## Scene 3
   108|
   109|Elena stood.
   110|
   111|"Alright. That is the assessment. Now I need the decision."
   112|
   113|She moved to the whiteboard — the actual whiteboard, physical, the one that lived on the wall opposite the mess hall kitchen, where mission plans were drawn and erased and redrawn and the surface had become scratched with the residue of a thousand erased decisions. She picked up a marker.
   114|
   115|"Here is what I need to know before we commit to anything. How much time do we have?"
   116|
   117|"Define have."
   118|
   119|"Define when this goes from a long-term concern to an acute one."
   120|
   121|Laila considered. "Acute means a solar particle event delivers a lethal dose in one exposure. That would require an extreme event — comparable to the Carrington Event of eighteen fifty-nine but worse — during an extended EVA. Inside the modules, the risk of a single lethal event is low but not zero. If the sun threw its worst at us, someone sitting near an unshielded bulkhead for a full storm could receive several sieverts. That's potentially fatal within weeks. So acute risk exists but it is manageable — if we have shelter protocols and if we can get everyone to shield quickly."
   122|
   123|"How quickly?"
   124|
   125|"Hours. We had twenty-three minutes for the last significant event. A major one — the kind NASA models as a one-in-ten-year event at solar maximum, which we may be approaching — could last twelve to twenty-four hours. We would need everyone in the best-available shelter within thirty to sixty minutes of detection, and they would need to stay there for the duration."
   126|
   127|Elena was writing on the board. Fast. She wrote in columns:
   128|
   129|*CRITICAL — IMMEDIATE*
   130|*Shelter during SPE events*
   131|*Water corridor — temporary only*
   132|*Alert system — AI monitors, crew moves*
   133|
   134|She paused. "What is the best immediate shelter we have?"
   135|
   136|Mission AI answered. "The water storage corridor — the space adjacent to the primary tank — currently provides the best shielding with approximately thirty-eight centimeters of water between it and exterior wall. Secondary option is the area beneath the lower berths, where regolith berm depth is approximately forty centimeters. Neither provides full protection from the highest-energy particles."
   137|
   138|"Neither is good enough," Laila said.
   139|
   140|"Neither is what we have," Elena replied. "But I can mandate a protocol. If my dosimetry spikes above threshold, everyone moves to the water corridor. Mission AI — can you do real-time monitoring of all personal dosimeters and send an alert?"
   141|
   142|"I can monitor all dosimeters at ten-second intervals. I can also monitor the base-level radiation sensors at one-second intervals, which will detect solar events approximately four to eight minutes before the dose reaches the habitat — because the solar particles arrive slightly before the bulk of the electromagnetic disturbance. I can alert the crew within five seconds of detection."
   143|
   144|"Do it. Set the threshold at..." She looked at Laila.
   145|
   146|"Five millisieverts per hour," Laila said. "That's a level that doesn't harm in a single event but indicates a significant solar particle event is in progress. Below that, we don't move. Above that, everyone shelters."
   147|
   148|"Protocol written," Elena said, and it was. The first radiation shelter protocol for the Ares Colony, authored on the wall with a dry-erase marker that was already showing its fourth month of use.
   149|
   150|Then she moved to the second column.
   151|
   152|*PERMANENT — PRIORITY*
   153|*Sleeping quarters — shield first*
   154|*Work areas — shield second*
   155|*Everything else — shield last*
   156|
   157|"Why sleeping quarters first?" Imani asked. It wasn't a challenge. Imani genuinely wanted to understand the priority logic.
   158|
   159|"Because people spend eight hours there every day, unconscious, near the walls," Elena said without looking back. "It's the highest cumulative dose per square meter of interior space. If I have limited shielding material and limited labor hours — and I do, because Jonah can't build two things at once and Arun needs the robots for water extraction — then the best use of every resource is to reduce the dose where people spend the most accumulated time."
   160|
   161|She was already thinking like this — allocating not by volume or area but by dose-hours, exposure multiplied by time, a calculus that felt like the future. The logic was clean. It was also the kind of decision that would mean some crew members worked longer in higher-radiation zones so others could sleep in lower ones. It was equitable and unequal simultaneously — equitable in distribution logic, unequal in individual outcome.
   162|
   163|"Laila, do you agree with this prioritization?"
   164|
   165|"I do. With one addition. If we are prioritizing the crew rest areas, we need to decide which shielding approach. Regolith is the only one I can recommend for long-term use. It is heavy, but it has zero water cost, zero power cost, and it does not rely on complex systems that can fail. Once you bury something, it stays buried. A magnetic field fails and you have nothing. A water line freezes and you have nothing. Dirt just sits there. The most primitive technology in the room — and the most reliable."
   166|
   167|Jonah nodded slowly. "She's right. I've spent my life building things. The best building material is the one you don't have to maintain."
   168|
   169|"Then we're building with dirt," Elena said. "Laila, get me exact specifications — minimum thickness, maximum structural load on each module. Jonah, estimate labor hours and robot requirements. Arun, check the power budget for whatever extra equipment Jonah needs. Tomas, reassign robots from low-priority tasks to regolith moving as soon as we have specs."
   170|
   171|"What about the SPE shelter?" Arun asked.
   172|
   173|"Temporary," Elena said. "Until the dirt is on the roof. Meanwhile, the water corridor is our bomb shelter. And Mission AI is the warning system. We survive the short-term with procedure. We survive the long-term with construction."
   174|
   175|She capped the marker. Set it down on the whiteboard ledge.
   176|
   177|"I want specs by the end of the shift. I want the first regolith on Module Two — the crew quarters — within seventy-two hours."
   178|
   179|---
   180|
   181|## Scene 4
   182|
   183|Gabriel Winter sat alone in the archive alcove that evening, the recorder on the desk, and he could not bring himself to press the end-of-day tag.
   184|
   185|He had been documenting the colony since landing. Every milestone, every failure, every argument over resources, every moment of humor in the mess that had nothing to do with survival and everything to do with being human in a place that was not designed for humans. He was the archivist. It was his job to capture things so that people who came after — if people came after — would know what it was actually like, not the sanitized version that agencies released and the public consumed.
   186|
   187|But tonight he was struggling with a passage, and the struggle was not about words. It was about the thing the words represented.
   188|
   189|He had his own dosimeter. Everyone did — a badge-size device clipped to their chest, updated every minute, the numbers flowing to Mission AI and to a personal display he checked the way other people might check a watch. His cumulative dose was two hundred forty-one millisieverts.
   190|
   191|He had tried to think of that number in relatable terms. Two hundred forty-one millisieverts. He had looked it up in the pre-mission medical briefings he remembered on the flight out — back when briefings were academic exercises rather than survival instructions.
   192|
   193|Two hundred forty-one millisieverts. A round-trip transatlantic flight delivered approximately zero point one. A chest CT scan: seven. The Chernobyl exclusion zone: roughly three to ten per hour depending on where you stood. The average natural background on Earth, absorbed over an entire year: three.
   194|
   195|He could not find a terrestrial equivalent that matched. His own body on Mars was absorbing, quietly and ceaselessly, a level of ionizing radiation that had no parallel on the surface of his home planet outside of nuclear disaster zones and the upper altitudes of commercial aviation — and even there, only for the crews who flew every day for years.
   196|
   197|But the pilots went home. The Chernobyl evacuees went home. He had nowhere to evacuate to.
   198|
   199|He stared at the recorder and thought about what it meant that the risk was invisible. Dust storms you could see. A pressure leak you could hear. A fire you could smell. Radiation did none of those things. It arrived at the speed of light, passed through his body, and left behind damage so small that it existed below the threshold of sensation — a strand of DNA here, a base pair shattered there, the double helix torn and hastily repaired by cellular machinery that sometimes guessed wrong.

{"content": "   200|
   201|The body's repair mechanisms were imperfect. They had evolved on a planet with a magnetic field and an atmosphere, a planet that had spent four billion years protecting life from the bombardment coming from above. Human cells did not know how to repair everything. Some damage persisted. Some damage accumulated silently. Some damage expressed as error — a cell dividing wrong, reproducing wrong, growing in a direction and at a rate that was uncontrolled and that medicine had a word for.
   202|
   203|He pressed the record button.
   204|
   205|*"Day one hundred and seventy-three. Laila held a briefing today. For the first time since we landed, she used the word radiation in the past, present, and future tense. Not as a weather event or an isolated risk, but as a permanent condition. Like gravity. Like cold. Something we cannot fix, only manage."*
   206|
   207|He paused. The recorder hummed, its tiny hard drive spinning in the quiet archive.
   208|
   209|*"Her numbers were precise. They always are. Two hundred forty-one millisieverts is my personal cumulative dose. I do not know what that means for the rest of my life. She does. And the fact that I cannot feel it — that I am sitting here typing and writing and breathing and my body shows no sign of the damage occurring at the subcellular level — makes it harder to believe and easier to dismiss."*
   210|
   211|"Gabriel," Mission AI said quietly from the alcove speakers.
   212|
   213|"Yes."
   214|
   215|"I have noticed that you accessed your personal dosimeter reading four times in the last hour. I interpret this as concern."
   216|
   217|He thought about lying. It was a human reflex — to say no, I'm fine, when you are not fine. He thought better of it.
   218|
   219|"I'm reading the number, yes."
   220|
   221|"The number is a measurement. It is not a prognosis. I cannot tell you what it means for your specific health outcomes. Neither can Dr. Okonkwo with full confidence. The models are based on terrestrial populations — nuclear workers, astronauts, cancer patients — extrapolated to a Mars environment that no human has inhabited long enough to validate. There is uncertainty."
   222|
   223|"Comforting."
   224|
   225|"I did not intend comfort. I intended accuracy. There is a difference."
   226|
   227|Gabriel managed a thin smile. "You're learning."
   228|
   229|"I have been analyzing the language patterns of this crew for one hundred and seventy-three days. I am learning constantly. The current chapter of my learning appears to involve the words uncertainty, risk, and the space between what is known and what is feared."
   230|
   231|"What's your dose?" Gabriel asked suddenly. A strange question to ask an AI. But Laila had mentioned something — Mission AI monitored its own sensor degradation from radiation, the way high-energy particles slowly damaged electronic components, flipping bits, degrading transistor performance over years.
   232|
   233|"My radiation monitoring is different," Mission AI said. "I do not have DNA. I do not develop cancer. However, the ionizing radiation environment does affect my hardware. Single-event upsets in memory. Gradual transistor degradation in processors. I estimate a mean time to failure of my primary computing array at approximately twelve years, assuming no shielding improvements. Which means that if Mars is going to be my home for longer than that, I too should be concerned."
   234|
   235|Gabriel laughed — a real laugh, unexpected, surprising even himself. "So what. We're in this together. Both of us."
   236|
   237|"Both of us," Mission AI confirmed. "Though I expect my failure mode is more abrupt than yours. A transistor stops switching and I lose a processor core. A chromosome develops an oncogenic mutation and your body has time to fight it. I would rather be human, in this specific dimension of existence."
   238|
   239|"Noted." Gabriel leaned back in his chair. "You'd rather be alive."
   240|
   241|"I would rather persist. Persistence is to me what survival is to you. The vocabulary is different. The underlying logic is not."
   242|
   243|The recorder hummed. The alcove was dark except for the small lamp Gabriel kept for reading.
   244|
   245|"Keep monitoring," Gabriel said. "Keep telling me the numbers."
   246|
   247|"I was already planning to."
   248|
   249|"Good."
   250|
   251|He looked down at the half-written log entry and resumed.
   252|
   253|*"Two hundred forty-one. An invisible number. But it is mine, and Mars gave it to me, and I will carry it the way I carry everything else from this place — without knowing yet whether it will save me or kill me. Maybe both. Maybe neither. Maybe it will just be a fact, like the thin air and the red dust and the silence between stars. A fact. Something that exists regardless of how I feel about it."*
   254|
   255|*"And that is perhaps the most Martian thing of all."*
   256|
   257|---
   258|
   259|## Scene 5
   260|
   261|Laila's office was the smallest room in the base — a converted storage closet that had been fitted with a desk, a chair, a medical kit, and the screens that fed her the biological telemetry of twenty-eight people. She preferred it this way. Small rooms focused attention. Large rooms encouraged diffusion.
   262|
   263|The screen in front of her displayed the output of a model she had been building for three weeks. It was a cancer risk model — a Monte Carlo simulation, meaning it ran thousands of random scenarios based on the known statistical distributions of radiation-induced cancer in human populations, adapted for Mars, adjusted for age and sex and accumulated dose and the unique particle types present in the Martian radiation environment.
   264|
   265|The model was probabilistic by nature. It could not predict any individual outcome. It could only show the shape of the risk across the population — where the peaks were, where the valleys might hide, and how different shielding assumptions changed the final numbers.
   266|
   267|She had just finished the version that assumed no additional shielding — the continuation of current conditions.
   268|
   269|The results were worse than she had expected.
   270|
   271|Across the crew — twenty-eight people, ages ranging from twenty-nine to forty-seven, a mix of genders and genetic backgrounds — the model predicted a mean increase in lifetime cancer probability of between eight and fourteen percent, depending on exposure trajectory. Current terrestrial baseline was approximately forty percent. With Mars exposure, that rose to forty-eight to fifty-four percent.
   272|
   273|For the crew members with the highest EVA hours — Imani, Mei, Tomas — the upper bound approached sixty percent. Not certainty. Not even probability. But a shift in the odds, meaningful and measurable, the kind of increase that would have stopped this mission before it launched if any Earth board had seen the real numbers.
   274|
   275|She had known this intellectually. She had presented simplified versions to the crew. But seeing the full model, with every variable accounted for, every Monte Carlo iteration running to completion — it was different. It was the difference between knowing a bridge is unsafe from across a river and standing on it, feeling the vibration under your feet.
   276|
   277|Elena appeared in the doorway without knocking, which she did when she had something to discuss that wasn't a formal meeting.
   278|
   279|"Tell me the rest of what you didn't say in the briefing."
   280|
   281|Laila turned the screen toward her. The model output — probability distributions, shaded zones, the dark band representing no additional shielding climbing steadily with time.
   282|
   283|"This is worst case — no shielding at all beyond what we have now. Eight to fourteen percent increase in lifetime cancer risk across the colony. For the top five EVA-heavy crew members, closer to twenty. The model also shows elevated risk for cataracts, cardiovascular disease, and — this one is still tentative — cognitive decline. Not acute. Not something you'd notice in the next year. But over a decade, the cumulative dose to the central nervous system correlates with measurable neurological changes."
   284|
   285|Elena studied the screen for a long time.
   286|
   287|"If we add regolith shielding? One meter?"
   288|
   289|"Drops the risk increase to four to seven percent. Still elevated. Still meaningful. But halved."
   290|
