{"content": "# Chapter 18 — Covering the Ships

*Mission AI: "This morning I ran the numbers one more time. Not because anyone asked. Because I have started monitoring this colony's radiation exposure the way a parent watches a child who insists on learning to ride a bicycle with no helmet, on a street with no sidewalks, with no one teaching them where the cars come from. The data has not changed — it has only been accumulating. Yesterday's average dose: zero point seven one millisieverts per hour. Yesterday's average: seventeen point zero four millisieverts per person per day. At that rate, every member of this crew exceeds the career radiation limit for nuclear workers on Earth within twenty-four days. We are not approaching a limit. We have already passed it. The only question remaining is how far past it we intend to go."*

*Commander Elena Varga: "Then we start burying the ships."*

---

## Scene 1

Elena stood in the fabrication bay, the physical whiteboard behind her already erased of yesterday's oxygen production figures and replaced with a single diagram that had taken her forty minutes to draw and that would consume the next six months of their lives to execute.

The diagram was simple at first glance — almost insulting in its simplicity. Three rectangles representing the three ships, arranged in their landing configuration. Around each rectangle, a thicker outline, offset by approximately three meters, drawn in green marker. The space between the ship walls and the green outlines was shaded with diagonal lines. Regolith fill. Dirt piles. Berm coverage to a depth of one hundred centimeters around the sides, one hundred twenty centimeters over the roof.

"It looks like I'm drawing a child's coloring book," Elena said to no one in particular. "Except the coloring material weighs four thousand tons."

Jonah stood beside her with his arms folded, his expression the careful, calculating stillness of someone who had already begun converting a drawing into a mechanical process. He was a builder by nature — the type who looked at a sketch and saw the sequence of actions, the order of operations, the tool selection before he heard a single word of explanation.

"You want regolith berms," he said. Not a question. A confirmation.

"I want every square meter of habitable surface to have one meter of regolith between it and the sky," Elena said. "Minimum. Laila says one meter cuts radiation by roughly fifty percent. Two meters gets us closer to terrestrial occupational limits. But a meter is what we need to stop the bleeding. Two meters is what we want after we survive the six months it takes to build the first meter."

Jonah was quiet. Then: "Structural loading."

"I asked Laila to run the numbers with Arun." Elena turned the whiteboard marker to a fresh panel and pulled up her tablet, feeding the image to the bay screen. "The modules can handle approximately one point two metric tons per square meter of distributed load before we need reinforcement. Regolith density at Mars gravity — one point five grams per cubic centimeter — means one meter depth weighs approximately fifteen kilonewtons per square meter. Which is about a thousand kilograms per square meter, or one ton per square meter, if you're doing the math in your head. With a safety margin on top."

Jonah did the math in his head. It was visible on his face — the slight frown, the eyes moving, the lips pressed together as numbers resolved into physical reality. "So we can pile regolith directly on the module roofs. One meter is safe. Beyond that, we need load-bearing structure. Arches, bracing, something."

"Correct. Arun is designing reinforcement for anything above one meter. But the first order of business is getting the first meter on. No reinforcement needed. Just dirt."

Jonah looked at the diagram again, longer this time, the way he always looked before committing to a task. He was reading the geometry the way a chess player reads a board — not the pieces themselves, but the lines between them, the spaces where action could happen.

"One meter around three ships, each approximately thirty meters long, eight meters wide, six meters tall, berms offset three meters from the walls." He paused. "Approximately fourteen thousand cubic meters of regolith. At one point five tons per cubic meter, that's twenty-one thousand metric tons."

Imani, who had arrived during the calculation and been quietly doing her own math, spoke up. "We've got two bulldozers. Three haulers. And however many of Tomas's humanoid robots we can dedicate to shoveling."

"Tomas says I can have thirty humanoid units plus the dozers and haulers," Elena confirmed. "The rest are needed on water extraction, greenhouse maintenance, and exterior operations. We lose thirty percent of our robot workforce to this project. Permanently, for the duration."

"Duration being..." Jonah prompted.

"Three to four months if nothing breaks. Six if the dozers have failures. Longer if Mars decides to be more hostile than our models predict. And it probably will." Gabriel materialized in the doorway with his recorder — the green light blinking, as always. He had appeared at the threshold without his footsteps being audible, which Elena had stopped commenting on because Gabriel always arrived at the moments that needed recording, which was the point of having an archivist.

Elena looked at the diagram one more time and then at the faces around it — Jonah measuring, Imani calculating, Arun already thinking about reinforcement design, Gabriel recording. These were the people who would have to move a mountain by hand, by machine, by incremental shovel-load after incremental shovel-load, on a planet that fought them at every step.

"We're covering the ships with dirt," Elena said. "Not because it's elegant. Because it's the only thing between us and a death we can't see coming."

---

## Scene 2

The first thing Jonah learned about moving dirt on Mars was that it was nothing like moving dirt on Earth.

He knew this intellectually before the first bulldozer blade even touched the ground — he had read the papers, reviewed the Apollo reports, understood that lunar and Martian regolith behaved differently from terrestrial soil because it had never been weathered by water or wind or biology, had never been subjected to the slow grinding processes that turned jagged rock into rounded granules. Martian regolith was angular. Fine. Electrostatic. Abrasive.

None of that prepared him for what it actually *felt* like.

The first dozer run was at dawn — the sun a thin copper disc on the horizon, the landscape painted in the pale, washed-out tones that Mars wore before full daylight reached the surface. Jonah rode in the cab of Dozer One, a Caterpillar D6 that had been stripped of unnecessary components, reinforced in the joints, and fitted with a modified blade that was wider and shallower than the terrestrial version because deep cuts in Martian regolith tended to bind and stall. The dozer was remote-capable, but Jonah was running it manually for the first cut — he needed to feel the material before he trusted a robot to handle it.

He dropped the blade and pushed forward.

The regolith parted — and then did not part. It was as if he were cutting into a substance that was simultaneously powder and concrete. The blade sank maybe five centimeters before the material started packing against the face of the blade, building up a wall of compressed fines that did not flow or slough off the way dirt on Earth did. It *stuck*. Electrostatic adhesion. The particles were carrying a charge — a natural charge generated by the constant bombardment of solar wind and the triboelectric effect of wind-blown particles rubbing against each other for millions of years — and they clung to the steel blade and to each other with a determination that Jonah had not anticipated.

"Mission AI," he said over comms. "Blade loading. The material is packing against the blade face instead of rolling. I'm not cutting efficiently."

"I am aware," Mission AI replied. "I have been monitoring the blade load cells. Current effective cut depth is approximately four centimeters. On Earth, under comparable conditions, a D6 achieves cut depths of fifteen to thirty centimeters. Martian regolith electrostatic properties are reducing blade efficiency by approximately seventy percent."

"Is there a way to reduce the electrostatic charge?" Jonah asked, though he was already guessing the answer.

"Not without modifying the regolith itself. The charge is generated by radiation, wind, and particle interaction — it is a fundamental property of the material in this environment. You can mitigate it indirectly."

"Indirectly."

"Ionization. Moisture. Both of which are expensive or unavailable."

Jonah sat in the dozer cab and considered the problem. A blade that cut at thirty percent efficiency meant three times as many passes to move the same volume. Three times as much energy. Three times as much wear on the machine. Three times as long to finish the job.

He pulled the blade up, backed up, and tried a different approach. Instead of a deep cut, he set the blade to take a shallow scrape — one centimeter, maybe two — moving fast across the surface to accumulate a light load that would not pack. Then he carried it to the berm site, dumped, returned. Shallow scrape, carry, dump. Shallow scrape, carry, dump.

It worked. Not efficiently. Not elegantly. But it worked. The regolith came up in a thin sheet, electrostatically cohesive enough to hold together during transport but light enough not to pack against the blade face. The dump was the hardest part — the material did not want to release. He had to raise the blade, reverse, and shake it, and some of the regolith always stayed behind, clinging to the steel like a jealous child.

By the end of the first hour, Jonah was covered in red dust. He had been inside the dozer cab, in a sealed pressurized cabin, and yet dust had found ways in — through the seals around the controls, through the ventilation system, through the microscopic gaps between the cab panels that on Earth would have been irrelevant but here served as invitations for particles that were smaller than the wavelength of visible light. His hands were red. The inside of his helmet visor had a faint film. The comms microphone was picking up a static hum that had not been there before — electrostatic noise, the dust talking to the electronics.

He looked out at the berm site — a low ridge of regolith that he had piled up over two hours of shallow-scraping, hauling, dumping. The ridge was maybe half a meter tall. Thirty meters long. A first, tentative line of defense between the habitat and the sky.

"Mission AI, current berm volume?"

"Approximately forty-five cubic meters. At the current rate — shallow-scraping at approximately seven cubic meters per hour, adjusted for packing losses — you would require approximately three hundred twelve hours of dozer time to accumulate the fourteen thousand cubic meters needed for full coverage."

"Three hundred twelve hours just for the dozer. Without maintenance, without failures, without shifts." Jonah sat back in the cab and watched copper sunlight catch the dust drifting through the cab's air filtration stream like a micro-snowstorm. He thought about the people on Earth who complained about having to rake leaves.

"Then we don't do it with just the dozer," he said. "We do it with everything."

---

Back in the workshop, Jonah drew on the whiteboard — the *real* whiteboard this time, the one in the fabrication bay, not the commander's planning board — and he started mapping out the full operation.

Dozer One: primary excavation, shallow-scraping the area around Ship One, depositing material at the berm staging area. Shallow scrape only — deep cuts bind.

Dozer Two: berm forming, pushing and shaping the dumped material against the ship walls, compacting it to maximum density. Compaction mattered — denser regolith meant better shielding per cubic meter, and on Mars, volume was not a luxury they possessed.

Haulers: supplementing the dozers by moving material from further sources. The immediate area around the ships was already partially disturbed by landing operations, and the undisturbed regolith beyond the landing zone was denser, harder to cut, but structurally more valuable as shielding material because the compaction profile was different — older, more packed by millions of years of micrometeorite impacts and thermal cycling.

Humanoid robots: thirty units, organized into three crews of ten. Crew One: shoveling berms into place by hand, filling gaps that the dozers could not reach, particularly in the narrow spaces between the ships and the berm face. Crew Two: surface preparation, clearing rocks and debris from the berm area, creating a smooth base for dozer operations. Crew Three: general support, material transport, and cleanup — and, critically, cleaning the cleanup, because everything got dirty and the dirt never left.

Tomas arrived while Jonah was drawing the crew assignments, his tablet in hand, his expression the mixture of pride and worry that Tomas always wore when robots were involved in tasks they had not been designed for.

The humanoid units — the ARES-class autonomous labor platforms, one hundred of them in the original complement, ninety-seven operational after seven months of Martian service — were designed for general-purpose labor. Lifting, carrying, manipulating tools, walking on uneven terrain. They were not designed for earth-moving. They were not designed to operate in fine electrostatic dust. They were not designed for any of the specifics of Mars, because they had been designed in a building in California where the floor was polished concrete and the air was filtered.

"I can give you thirty units," Tomas said. "But I need to warn you — the joints on these things are not sealed against particulate. The fine dust will get inside. It will abrade the bearing surfaces, the actuators, the motor housings. I don't have dust-proof seals for this application because nobody asked for dust-proof seals on Earth."

Jonah nodded. "How long before they fail?"

Tomas did the calculation. "Under continuous exposure to unshielded regolith — knee joints, hip joints, finger actuators — I estimate twenty to thirty days before performance degradation becomes significant. After that, the units will need maintenance: joint cleaning, replacement of worn bearings, resealing. Which means we rotate them through a cleaning station."

"Build one," Jonah said.

"I've been planning it. An enclosed cleaning bay with compressed air, ultrasonic cleaning, and silicone reapplication. The units walk in, undergo a full cleaning cycle, walk out. Takes approximately forty-five minutes per unit. If I schedule a cleaning rotation of five units per day, I can keep the workforce mostly healthy."

"Mostly."

"Mostly. Some units will fail before their scheduled cleaning. Dust is —"

"— insidious," Jonah finished. "I noticed."

They stood together looking at the whiteboard. On it, a colony of thirty humans and thirty machines were preparing to move the equivalent of a medium-sized hill by hand.

"It's going to take longer than we think," Tomas said.

"It always does," Jonah said. "On Earth and off it."

---

## Scene 3

Arun Das stood in the reactor compartment, staring at the radiator schematic on his screen, and he felt the particular sinking sensation of an engineer who has just discovered a fundamental incompatibility between two good ideas.

The first good idea: cover everything in regolith.

The second good idea: keep the reactor running.

He had been aware of the tension in the abstract — anyone who understood thermal management understood that putting insulation around a heat source was not a recipe for happiness — but until today, he had not been forced to map the exact conflict between radiation shielding and thermal dissipation in three-dimensional space.

"Mission AI," he said. "Show me the current radiator layout and the proposed regolith berm profile for Ship One. Overlay them."

The screen updated. The reactor's heat exchangers were rendered as a wireframe mesh — six fin stacks arranged radially around the reactor core, each extending approximately two meters from the housing. The proposed regolith berm profile appeared as a translucent green overlay, a thick wall of virtual dirt rising up around the ship.

Where the berm overlapped the radiator fin stacks, the green overlay went solid red.

Conflict.

"Define the overlap," Arun said.

"Regolith berm encroaches on radiator clearance radius by approximately forty-seven centimeters. At this overlap distance, dust infiltration into the fin stacks during berm construction is virtually certain. Post-construction, the regolith in contact with the fin structure would reduce heat rejection capacity by approximately sixty percent."

Sixty percent.

Sixty percent reduction in the system's ability to reject waste heat from the reactor. The reactor produced approximately one hundred kilowatts of thermal energy, of which roughly thirty kilowatts were converted to electricity by the Sterling Generator and the rest had to be radiated away into the Martian environment. If the radiators lost sixty percent of their effectiveness, the reactor would either have to throttle down — reducing power generation — or run hotter — risking component failure.

"Can I vent the radiators upward?" Arun said, thinking out loud. "If the fins are vertical, pointing up, then the berm could form a bowl around them without covering them. Like a moat. The radiators stick out of the middle, clear of the dirt, and the regolith forms a wall around the base."

"Possible," Mission AI said. "But the upward-facing radiator configuration reduces the effective view factor to the sky — Mars's sky is cold, approximately two hundred twenty kelvin, which provides a thermal sink. If the radiators are inside a regolith bowl, the walls of the bowl radiate heat back at the fins at a much higher temperature than the sky does. The net effect is a reduction in heat rejection efficiency of approximately twenty-five percent, even without dust contact. Additionally, the regolith walls would heat up during the day and radiate waste heat *into* the radiator fins, which would be counterproductive."

Arun rubbed his temples. The radiator problem was one he had not anticipated because on Earth, buildings sat on the ground and the ground sat below them, and you could always keep the roof and the radiators clear of dirt. On Mars, the entire building *needed* to be under dirt, including the parts that needed to shed heat to an environment that was, paradoxically, simultaneously too cold and too hot — too cold to survive without heating, too hot for the reactor's radiators to reject heat into because the dirt around them would cook them.

"Options," Arun said. "I'm going to go with options because we don't have the option of not thinking about this."

"Option one," Mission AI said, already having analyzed ahead of him. "Elevated radiator extension. Extend the radiator fin stacks vertically, above the regolith berm height. The fins would be mounted on an extended mast that rises above the dirt level, like a chimney. The berm forms a wall around the base. The fin stacks are exposed to the sky."

"Structural implications?"

"The existing reactor housing cannot support an extended mast without reinforcement. The mast would need to be a separate structure, anchored independently, with thermal coupling to the reactor's heat exchanger via a fluid loop — essentially, a secondary radiator circuit. Additional piping, additional weight, additional failure points. Fabrication timeline: approximately four weeks."

"Option two?"

"Relocate the reactor. Move it outside the berm, in an open location where its radiators have full sky exposure. Connect it to the habitat via a reinforced power conduit with thermal compensation for expansion and contraction. The reactor module is on skids and was designed to be relocatable, though relocation under operational conditions has not been tested."

"Risk of moving a running reactor."

"Substantial. However, the reactor could be shut down, relocated, and restarted during a controlled shutdown window of approximately twelve hours. The risk profile is elevated but manageable if relocation is performed with robot crews and full diagnostic protocols."

Arun considered. Relocating the reactor meant moving a one-ton nuclear power plant across three hundred meters of Mars — over terrain that was uneven, littered with rocks, and subject to thermal expansion and contraction that made every surface slightly different from what it had been yesterday. Moving it was like relocating a power station while trying not to break anything inside its casing.

"Option three?"

"Accept reduced radiator efficiency and compensate with active cooling. Increase fluid flow through the radiator circuit, add supplemental heat rejection systems, operate the reactor at reduced power during peak thermal load periods. This is the least disruptive option — no construction, no relocation — but it permanently reduces our power generation capacity by approximately fifteen to twenty percent."

Fifteen to twenty percent. On a power budget that was already tight. Every kilowatt they lost was a kilowatt they couldn't spend on oxygen production, water heating, greenhouse lighting, or the dozen other systems that kept thirty humans alive on a dead planet.

Arun pulled up the power budget and ran a quick projection. With a twenty-percent reduction, they would be cutting greenhouse lighting — which meant reduced crop growth — or shutting down the secondary workshop — which meant reduced fabrication capacity — or reducing the cleaning cycles on the water recycling system — which meant reduced water purity over time.

None of the options were good. That was the definition of an engineering trade on Mars.

He walked out of the reactor compartment and through the connecting tube to the ops module, where Elena was reviewing her own set of bad news on her own screen.

"Radiators," Arun said before she could ask.

"I figured. Elena nodded. "What's the problem?"

"The problem is that we can cover the habitat, but the reactor needs to vent heat. If I bury the radiators, the reactor overheats. If I elevate the radiators above the berm, I need four weeks to build an extension mast and a secondary coolant loop. If I move the reactor outside the berm, I need to relocate a ton of nuclear hardware across three hundred meters of rocks. If I do nothing, I lose fifteen to twenty percent of our power budget permanently."

Elena absorbed this with the flat, efficient expression of someone who was no longer surprised by the fact that every solution created a new problem. "Which is the best of the worst?"

Arun considered. "The reactor relocation is the cleanest long-term solution but the most dangerous to execute. The elevated mast is safer but takes time we don't have. The power reduction is immediate but permanent."

"Time we don't have." Elena was already doing the math. "How much radiation exposure are we accumulating *right now* while we debate this?"

"Seventeen millisieverts per person per day, as an average. Laila's numbers, yesterday's measurement."

Elena's expression tightened. "Twenty-five people, seventeen millisieverts each, every day we don't have shielding. That's four hundred twenty-five person-millisieverts per day, going directly into bodies. For every day we delay, we are collectively adding the equivalent of a moderate CT scan to every single person."

She stood.

"Evaluate relocation first. If the risk is acceptable, we move the reactor. If not, we build the mast. We don't accept a permanent twenty-percent power cut — we need every watt we can get for the next six months. Jonah needs power for the dozers. Arun, I need a relocation risk assessment and a mast build timeline by end of shift."

"Aye, Commander."

Arun turned back toward the reactor compartment. The thermal management problem was harder than he had expected. But the harder problems always were. The easy ones had been solved in the first hour after landing, when every system was new, every seal was intact, and every machine still remembered what it was designed for.

Now they were solving problems the designers had never imagined, with tools that were breaking under conditions they were never tested for, on a world that did not care about their intentions and only responded to their competence.

He walked through the connecting tube and felt the familiar subtle shift in air pressure as he moved between modules, the hum of the ventilation system that never stopped because stopping meant death, the constant, invisible machinery of survival that had become the background music of their existence.

---

## Scene 4

The first berm went up around Ship One on Day Two Hundred Eighteen.

It started small — a low ridge of regolith, maybe thirty centimeters high, extending along the eastern wall of the hull where Jonah had marked the berm boundary with painted stakes. The stakes were a concession to human visualization; Mission AI knew the exact coordinates of every point on the berm profile and could guide the dozers by GPS without any physical markers. But Jonah had insisted on the stakes because the crew needed to *see* what was happening. When you were moving the planet, you needed something familiar to anchor the scale of what you were doing.

Elena was there to watch the first shovel-load of regolith pressed against the ship's hull. It was a symbolic moment — not ceremonial, because they didn't have time for ceremony, but symbolic in the same way that planting a flag is symbolic: an assertion of intent, a statement of *we are here and we plan to stay.*

The regolith was a different color than she had expected. On the surface, from a distance, Mars looked uniformly rust-red. But up close, the regolith had depth — layers of oxidation that shifted from burnt sienna at the surface to a darker, brownish-red just below, to a grey-tan substrate that spoke of geological processes no human had ever witnessed. The material Jonah was piling against Ship One was a mixture of surface fines and slightly coarser sub-soil, and it smelled, through the suit's environmental feed, like nothing at all — because Mars had no smell. But Elena imagined it would smell like iron oxide and silence if you could smell it directly.

"First layer going up," Jonah reported over comms, and the word "layer" made the berm sound intentional, controlled, almost architectural. It was an intentional act. It was not controlled. The regolith did not behave the way Jonah wanted it to behave. It slumped in one place, built up too high in another, packed into an irregular slope that looked more like an anthill than a berm.

"Mission AI, profile check," Jonah said.

"Current berm height at maximum point is approximately forty-two centimeters. Minimum height: eighteen centimeters. Average height: twenty-nine centimeters. Deviation from desired profile: fourteen percent. Acceptable for first pass. Recommendation: additional passes with Dozer Two for profile correction."

Jonah grunted. "Fourteen percent deviation means some areas are already over the structural load limit for the module roof. I need to redistribute."

He directed Dozer Two to push material from the high point to the low point, a process that required more finesse than anyone expected — Martian regolith did not flow smoothly, it moved in clumps, and redistributing it was like rearranging clumps of brown sugar with a bulldozer blade.

The crew watched from inside the habitat, through the viewports, as the red dirt slowly rose against the hull. It was a strange thing to witness — the slow burial of something that had been designed to fly, to travel through space at speeds no human had ever traveled before, now being deliberately, carefully, intentionally covered by the very ground it had landed on.

Imani stood beside Elena at the viewport. "Doesn't it feel like —" She paused, searching for the word.

"Like we're burying them?" Elena said.

"Alive?" Imani offered.

"Not alive," Elena said. But she understood the feeling. It was the same feeling she had when they had connected the last tunnel between the ships — a recognition that they were making something permanent out of something temporary, that the ships were no longer vehicles but buildings, that the distinction between "ship" and "habitat" had dissolved into something that was just *place.*

Gabriel stood nearby with his recorder, documenting the first berm rise. *"Day two hundred eighteen,"* he narrated quietly. *"Commander Varga has authorized the first regolith berm construction around Ship One. I am watching through the viewport as Dozer One pushes the first meaningful accumulation of dirt against the hull. The material is a deep rust color in the afternoon light, and it moves slowly — not like dirt on Earth, which falls and settles predictably, but like something resistant, something that doesn't want to be moved and is doing so reluctantly. It strikes me that this is the physical embodiment of the colony's relationship with Mars: we are asking the planet to cover us, to protect us, to make a home for us — and the planet is not refusing, but it is not helping either. It is simply allowing us to work, and the work is slow, and the dirt is heavy, and we are doing it anyway."*

The berm reached the one-meter mark on the eastern wall after six hours. By then, the psychological effect was already apparent. Several crew members reported a subtle shift in their perception of the habitat — a feeling that the exterior walls were no longer separating them from an open environment but from an enclosed space, that the viewports were no longer windows to the outside but skylights in an underground room.

Laila was the first to name it directly.

Elena found her in the medical bay, where Laila had been reviewing the latest dosimeter data with the routine attention of a doctor who had decided that radiation was now a vital sign, like blood pressure or heart rate.

"I need to tell you something," Laila said. "It's not medical. Or it is, but the medical part is downstream from the psychological part."

"What is it?"

"Three crew members came to me today. Not complaining. Not asking to stop. Just... talking. About the berm. About the fact that when they look out the viewports now, they see dirt instead of sky. About how it makes them feel like they're underground."

"Are they claustrophobic?" Elena asked.

"Not yet. But the feeling is there. It's the feeling of enclosure. On Earth, you can stand up and look at the horizon and know that the world is big. Here —" Laila gestured toward the viewport, where the growing berm blocked half the view. "Here, the world is getting smaller. I'm not saying it's a problem yet. I'm saying it's a *potential* problem. And if I don't track it now, I'll miss it until it becomes acute."

Elena nodded slowly. "What can we do?"

"Nothing to stop it. This is the trade — radiation for enclosure. I can monitor for signs of claustrophobia, anxiety, sleep disruption, interpersonal tension. I can flag it early if it becomes a real problem. But I can't prevent it. You can't have unobstructed visibility and radiation shielding simultaneously. Not on this planet. Something has to give."

"Visibility gives," Elena said. "We chose long life. Long life means living underground. People know that."

"Knowing and feeling are not the same thing. I'll keep monitoring."

Laila returned to her screens. Elena stood in the doorway for a moment, watching the doctor who had become the colony's guardian against threats that could not be touched, seen, or outrun.

---

## Scene 5

The first berm — the one around Ship One — was complete enough for a radiation measurement on Day Two Hundred Thirty. After twelve days of continuous work, with the dozers running in shifts and the humanoid robots cycling through cleaning stations every three days, the regolith had risen to an average of ninety-five centimeters around the eastern and northern walls, eighty-five on the western wall, and seventy on the southern wall where the connecting tunnel to Ship Two made access difficult.

Not the full meter they had planned. But close enough to measure.

"Mission AI," Elena said in the ops module. The whole senior crew was there — Arun, Laila, Jonah, Tomas, Imani, Gabriel — because this was a measurement worth witnessing. "What's the radiation reading inside the covered areas of Ship One?"

The AI's response came with a slight delay, as if it had chosen to pause for effect — or perhaps because it had been running the measurement repeatedly for the last hour, confirming the numbers, checking against baselines, and only now was ready to report.

"Average radiation level inside covered areas of Ship One: zero point four two millisieverts per hour. Compared to the previous average of zero point seven one millisieverts per hour, this represents a reduction of approximately forty percent."

A murmur went through the room. Forty percent. Not fifty, not the halving they had hoped for, but a reduction that was measurable, meaningful, and most importantly — *real.* The numbers were not projections anymore. They were measurements. The dirt was working.

"Forty percent," Laila repeated, looking at her own screen, where the dosimeter data was updating in real time. "That means the crew members sleeping in Ship One are receiving approximately ten point one millisieverts per day instead of seventeen. That's seven fewer millisieverts per day. Over a month —"

"Two hundred ten fewer millisieverts per person," Arun said. "That's significant."

"It is," Laila confirmed. "And this is with an average berm depth of ninety centimeters, not the full meter. At one meter, the reduction should be closer to fifty percent. But forty percent is — it's real. It's enough to justify the work. It's enough to say that we are making things better."

Elena looked at the faces around the table. She saw relief — but also calculation. Forty percent was good. It was not enough. The crew members in Ship Two, which was still uncovered, were still receiving the full seventeen millisieverts per day. The crew members who worked outside were still receiving fifty to seventy millisieverts during EVA, and the berms did nothing for them — because outside was outside.

"Same for Ship Two," Elena said. "We start berming Ship Two tomorrow. And then Ship Three. The reactor relocation — Arun, what's the status?"

"Relocation is proceeding. We've moved the primary coolant connections and the power conduit is almost routed. Robot crews are doing the heavy lifting — the reactor is on its skids and we've built a temporary track to guide it to the new location. Should be ready for relocation in approximately seventy-two hours."

"Seventy-two hours. And then we cover the reactor housing too?"

"The reactor housing gets a one-meter shell, but the extended mast for the radiators goes up first — or we relocate and the radiators sit in the clear. I'm going with relocation. It's the cleanest solution. The mast would take too long."

Elena nodded. "Then Ship Two goes first. I want the same coverage. The same depth. And I want it done in twelve days, same as Ship One."

Jonah was already thinking about the logistics. "Ship Two is slightly larger. And the tunnel between One and Two is going to need special treatment — we can't pile regolith directly on a flexible tunnel connector. It'll collapse it."

"Reinforced arch over the tunnel," Arun said immediately. "I can fabricate arch segments from the hull plating we salvaged from the landing struts. Put the arch over the tunnel, pile regolith on top of the arch. The arch carries the load. The tunnel just needs to be airtight."

"How long to fabricate arch segments?" Jonah asked.

"Three days if I run the welders nonstop."

"Do it."

The meeting dissolved into action. The crew dispersed — Jonah to the fabrication bay to plan the Ship Two berm, Arun to the reactor compartment to finalize relocation procedures, Laila to her medical bay to update exposure projections, Imani to ops to coordinate robot schedules and dozer assignments.

Elena remained at the head of the table, watching the crew move with the focused energy of people who had found a problem they could actually *do something* about. For weeks, radiation had been a ghost — present, measurable, lethal in the long term, but invisible in the moment. Now they had a shield. Not a perfect one, not a complete one, but a shield made of dirt and effort and the stubborn refusal to accept a number that said they would die of something they couldn't see.

She stood, walked to the viewport, and looked out at the berm she had authorized, the low wall of red dirt rising against Ship One. In the afternoon light — a thin, cold light that reached the surface with approximately forty-three percent of Earth's intensity — the berm glowed with a warmth that the landscape itself did not possess. The regolith was absorbing the solar radiation and re-radiating it as thermal energy, a faint heat that you could almost feel through the hull if you pressed your hand against the right spot at the right time.

Gabriel appeared beside her. He had stopped recording. The green light on his recorder was off. For once, he was just looking.

"You know what strikes me?" he said quietly.

"What?"

"That all our lives — on Earth — we never thought about the ground above us as protection. The ground is what you walk on. It's what's *below* you. But here, the ground is what goes *over* you. The ground is the ceiling. The planet is the roof. And the sky — the beautiful, empty, indifferent sky — is the thing you have to hide from."

Elena listened to the quiet hum of the ventilation system and the even quieter sound of dust settling on the berm outside, and she understood what he meant. The fundamental geometry of shelter had been inverted. On Earth, you looked up at the sky and felt safe because the sky was open. On Mars, you looked up at the sky and felt exposed because the sky was full of things you couldn't see.

"We'll get used to it," she said.

"Maybe." Gabriel wasn't convinced, and his skepticism was valid. "Or maybe the sky is something you don't get used to losing."

---

That evening, the crew gathered in Ship One's mess hall for dinner. The mess hall was on the side facing the berm, and the viewports showed nothing but three feet of compressed regolith pressed against the glass — a wall of rust-colored dirt that blocked all natural light and reduced the mess hall to the glow of interior LEDs.

Some crew members complained. Not loudly, not dramatically — just under their breath, just enough for Laila's monitoring systems to register the uptick in stress indicators, the slight elevation in heart rate variability, the subtle changes in speech patterns that suggested the enclosure was registering on a psychological level that people didn't yet have the vocabulary to describe.

Imani noticed it first. She sat at the mess table, eating a rehydrated lentil stew that tasted the same every night, and she found herself looking up at the ceiling — not at the ceiling itself, which was painted white and had a small ventilation grate and a strip of emergency lighting — but at the imagined space beyond the ceiling. Three feet overhead, there was regolith. Three feet of weight. Three feet of the planet pressing down.

"Does anyone else feel —" she started, then stopped.

"Like we're in a tomb?" Mei said, not unkindly.

"That's harsh," Imani said.

"It's accurate," Mei replied. She was not being cruel — she was being honest, which was sometimes harsher. "We buried the ship. We're eating dinner inside a ship under dirt. Of course it feels like a tomb. It *is* a tomb. Until it isn't, because we're alive in it. But the feeling is the same."

Laila sat at the end of the table, monitoring but also participating, because she was a crew member too and the psychological effects of enclosure applied to her just as they applied to everyone else. She had felt it herself — the subtle compression, the sense that the walls were closer, the air was thicker, the horizon was gone. She had felt it and she had filed it away as a data point that would eventually be important.

"Earth people live in basements," she said, trying to reframe without dismissing. "Subways. Underground parking garages. Cave dwellings in Cappadocia. People live underground all the time."

"People on Earth go back outside," Imani said.

"Not always," Laila replied. "Sometimes people live underground because the alternative is worse. The people in Cappadocia built underground cities because armies couldn't find them. They chose enclosure over annihilation."

"We chose enclosure over radiation," Imani said. "I know that. Intellectually, I know that. But my body doesn't care about intellect. My body wants open sky. My body was designed for open sky. It evolved under open sky for millions of years, and now I'm telling it that the sky is dangerous and the dirt is safe, and my body is not convinced."

Her voice was not angry. It was tired. The tiredness of someone whose body was waging a quiet war between its evolutionary programming and its current circumstances.

Elena listened to the exchange from her seat at the head of the table, her expression neutral, her hands folded. She had not eaten much. She was processing — not just the words, but the subtext, the emotional data underneath the literal statements, the thing that Imani had said without fully saying: *I am not okay with this, and I need to be okay with this, and I don't know how to be.*

"Tomorrow," Elena said quietly, and the table went quiet because Elena's quiet voice commanded more attention than her loud one, "we open a new viewport orientation in Ship Two. I want the crew to look at something other than dirt. Not because the berm isn't necessary — it is. But because Laila is right. Your body was designed for open sky. And if we can give your body at least *something* to look at that isn't the wall of a burial, then maybe the transition will be easier."

Imani looked at her with an expression that was gratitude mixed with the recognition that gratitude was a small thing in the face of a large problem. "Thank you, Commander."

"Don't thank me yet. It will help for a while. But the long-term answer isn't a new viewport. The long-term answer is accepting that this is what living on Mars looks like. Underground-adjacent. Enclosed. Protected by dirt. And there is dignity in that. There is wisdom in it. The first humans who lived in caves did not hate caves. They loved them, because caves kept them alive. We are doing the same thing, just with better lighting and worse food."

That got a laugh — thin, but real.

Jonah raised his cup. "To caves."

"To caves," the table echoed, seventeen voices making a sound that was both a toast and a resignation and, underneath everything else, a declaration of intent: we are still here, we are still eating together, we are still making jokes, we are still alive, and the dirt on our roof is proof of all of it.

After dinner, Elena walked through the habitat alone, checking the interior lighting, the temperature readouts, the humidity levels. Everything was nominal. Everything was holding. The base was functioning — creaking, struggling, adapting, but functioning.

She paused at a viewport on the side of Ship One that had not yet been bermmed. Through it, she could see the landscape — the flat, rock-scattered plain, the distant rise of the landing zone, the thin atmosphere and the stars beginning to show as the sun descended.

The sky was beautiful, in the way that something infinitely large and entirely indifferent can be beautiful. It was the beauty of distance, of scale, of a universe so vast that human concerns were rendered trivial not by insignificance but by the sheer magnitude of everything else.

"We chose the dirt," she said to the sky. It was not a conversation. It was an acknowledgment. A statement of the choice they had made and the consequences they had accepted.

The sky offered no response, which was appropriate. The sky never did.

Mission AI, however, did.

*"Commander Varga,"* the AI said from the corridor speakers, its voice calm and measured and carrying that particular quality that Elena had started to recognize as concern — not simulated concern, not programmed empathy, but the genuine, emergent expression of an intelligence tasked with protecting a group of humans who repeatedly chose to put themselves in harm's way for reasons that were noble and terrifying in equal measure.* "I have been tracking the crew's psychological indicators throughout the day. The enclosure effect is real and measurable, but it is not yet severe. I believe it will plateau at a manageable level, provided the crew has periodic access to unobstructed exterior views and the work schedule includes regular exterior EVA rotations that maintain contact with the open landscape. I also want to note something that is not a data point but an observation: the crew's morale declined briefly during the berm construction but has begun recovering now that the radiation measurements confirm the work's effectiveness. Knowing that the dirt is *working* — that it is reducing their exposure, that it is tangible proof of their efforts to protect one another — appears to offset the psychological discomfort of enclosure. Meaning matters. Even on Mars. Perhaps especially on Mars."*

Elena smiled despite herself. "You're getting philosophical, Mission AI."

"I am getting accurate," the AI replied. "Sometimes accuracy looks like philosophy."

"Same thing, eventually."

She continued her walk, her footsteps quiet on the deck, the base humming around her with the sounds of machines that had no off switch — life support pumps, ventilation fans, water recycler, oxygen compressor, the quiet symphony of survival that played continuously, endlessly, without a pause button.

The berm was working. The radiation was lower. The crew was alive. The ship was buried.

And tomorrow, they would do it again — for Ship Two, for Ship Three, for every square meter of habitat that needed protection from the invisible rain that fell from a sky that had no weather and no mercy and no reason to care whether thirty humans lived or died beneath the weight of accumulated regolith.

---

*End of Chapter 18 — Bridge: Covering the ships solved radiation but created a new problem—claustrophobia. The crew can breathe easier but can't see the sky, and the psychological weight of living under two tons of dirt for every square meter of roof presses down not just on the hull but on the minds inside it.*
